body:
Why complex organisms need transport systems

In a single-celled organism, many substances can move over short distances across the cell surface. In a large multicellular organism, distant cells cannot depend on diffusion alone for an adequate supply of nutrients and oxygen. Specialised transport systems distribute useful substances and collect wastes.

Blood and the circulatory system

The human circulatory system consists mainly of the heart, blood and blood vessels. The heart is a muscular pump with 4 chambers: 2 atria that receive blood and 2 ventricles that pump it onward.

Blood contains a liquid component called plasma and several cellular components:

  • Red blood cells: Contain haemoglobin, which carries most of the oxygen transported in blood.
  • White blood cells: Participate in protecting the body against infections.
  • Platelets: Help blood clot after injury.
  • Plasma: Transports dissolved substances such as nutrients, hormones and some waste products.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins return blood towards it. Capillaries are very small vessels where exchange with body tissues occurs.

The terms artery and vein describe the direction of blood flow relative to the heart, not a fixed oxygen content. The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart.

Double circulation in humans

Human blood passes through 2 linked circulatory routes. In pulmonary circulation, blood travels from the right side of the heart to the lungs and returns to the left side. In systemic circulation, oxygen-rich blood travels from the left side of the heart to the body and oxygen-poor blood returns to the right side.

This arrangement helps keep oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood largely separate in the normal adult circulation and provides an effective supply of oxygen to body tissues.

Excretion removes metabolic wastes

Cells produce waste substances during metabolism. Carbon dioxide is removed mainly through the lungs. Urea, a nitrogen-containing waste formed mainly in the liver during the processing of amino acids, is removed principally through the kidneys.

Each kidney contains numerous microscopic functional units called nephrons. Blood is filtered, and useful substances and much of the water are selectively reabsorbed. The remaining urine passes through the ureters into the urinary bladder and leaves the body through the urethra.

Excretion is different from egestion. Urine contains metabolic wastes removed from blood; faeces chiefly contain undigested material and other substances passing through the digestive tract.

How plants transport substances

Plants do not have a heart or blood. They possess conducting tissues:

TissueMain materialUsual transport pattern
XylemWater and dissolved mineral nutrientsPrimarily from roots towards stems and leaves
PhloemSugars and other organic substancesFrom food-producing or storage regions to parts that need them

Water absorbed by roots moves through xylem. The evaporation of water from above-ground plant surfaces, mainly through stomata, is called transpiration. Transpiration contributes to the upward movement of water and helps cool the plant, but excessive loss can cause water stress.

Phloem transport is called translocation. Sugars can move from leaves to developing fruits or roots, and stored sugars can move from storage organs towards growing shoots. Its direction depends on which region supplies sugars and which region requires them.

Transpiration, photosynthesis and respiration are 3 different processes. Transpiration is primarily water loss as vapour; photosynthesis manufactures organic food using light; respiration releases usable energy in living cells.

Prelims focus

  • The human heart has 4 chambers and supports pulmonary and systemic circulation.
  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it towards the heart.
  • The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood, while pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood.
  • Nephrons are the functional units of the kidneys.
  • Xylem mainly transports water and minerals; phloem transports organic food materials.
  • Trap: Excretion of metabolic wastes is not the same as egestion of undigested food.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 11, Transportation in Animals and Plants, sections 11.1–11.3; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 6, Life Processes, sections on transportation and excretion; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Chapters 18 and 19, Body Fluids and Circulation and Excretory Products and Their Elimination.]

pictures.caption: Human circulation includes a pulmonary route through the lungs and a systemic route through the body.

title: Transport, Circulation and Excretion in Plants and Animals

body:
Habitat and adaptation

A habitat is the natural place where an organism lives and obtains the conditions and resources it needs. A pond, forest, grassland and desert are examples of habitats. Their conditions differ, so the organisms inhabiting them often have different structures and behaviours.

An adaptation is an inherited characteristic that increases an organism's ability to survive or reproduce in its environment. Adaptations evolve in populations over many generations through processes such as natural selection. They may involve body structure, physiological functioning or behaviour.

Biotic and abiotic conditions

Every habitat contains biotic components, including plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms, and abiotic components, including water, temperature, light, air and soil.

Abiotic factors influence where organisms can live. For example, limited rainfall restricts plant growth in deserts, whereas oxygen availability and salinity influence life in aquatic habitats. Organisms also respond to predators, competitors, food sources and disease-causing organisms.

Structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations

TypeMeaningExample
StructuralA physical feature of the bodyFish have streamlined bodies that reduce resistance during swimming.
PhysiologicalA feature of internal functioningCamels conserve water through highly concentrated urine and dry dung.
BehaviouralA characteristic pattern of activityMany desert animals remain in burrows during the hottest part of the day.

Adaptations to important habitats

Hot and dry habitats

Water conservation is particularly important where rainfall is low and evaporation is high. Many cacti have reduced leaves or spines, thick outer coverings and green water-storing stems. These features reduce water loss and help the plants tolerate drought.

Camels have broad, padded feet suited to sandy ground and can tolerate substantial changes in body water. Their ability to produce concentrated urine and dry dung helps conserve water. A camel's hump stores fat, not a reservoir of liquid water.

Cold mountain habitats

Thick fur provides insulation in animals such as yaks. Many high-altitude conifers have narrow, needle-like leaves and sloping branches that help them withstand cold conditions and shed snow. Mountain animals may also possess specialised feet or hooves suited to rocky or snowy ground.

Aquatic habitats

Most fish have gills that obtain oxygen from water. Their streamlined bodies and fins assist movement. Whales and dolphins are different because they are mammals with lungs; they must periodically surface to breathe air.

Aquatic plants may have flexible stems, floating leaves or finely divided submerged leaves. These features can support access to light and movement in water. Their exact form depends on whether the plant is floating, rooted or fully submerged.

Coastal wetlands

Mangroves are plants adapted to coastal intertidal environments where tidal flooding, salinity and oxygen-poor mud create special challenges. Some mangrove species possess specialised roots that assist gas exchange. Salt management also differs among species.

Gujarat has important mangrove ecosystems along the Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat. Their vegetation provides habitat for aquatic organisms and contributes to shoreline protection. This illustrates how plant adaptations can influence the functioning of an entire coastal ecosystem.

Adaptation versus acclimatisation

Acclimatisation is a physiological adjustment made by an individual during its lifetime in response to changed conditions. A person travelling from the plains to a high mountain may initially breathe faster and later adjust partly to the reduced oxygen availability. This does not mean that the person's species has evolved a new inherited adaptation within a few days.

FeatureAdaptationAcclimatisation
Biological basisInherited characteristics shaped across generationsAdjustment within an individual's lifetime
Time scaleGenerally many generationsUsually comparatively short
ExampleFish gills used for gas exchange in waterPhysiological adjustment after moving to high altitude

Adaptation is not a conscious decision made by an organism. Useful inherited variations can become more common in populations over generations. Acclimatisation, by contrast, is a change in an individual's functioning under changed conditions.

Prelims focus

  • A habitat includes both biotic and abiotic components.
  • Adaptations may be structural, physiological or behavioural.
  • Cacti conserve water through features such as reduced leaves and thick stems.
  • Fish obtain oxygen mainly through gills; whales and dolphins use lungs.
  • Mangroves occur in Gujarat's coastal ecosystems, including the Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Trap: Acclimatisation of an individual is not the same as inherited adaptation across generations.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 9, The Living Organisms—Characteristics and Habitats, sections 9.2–9.3; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 7, Weather, Climate and Adaptations of Animals to Climate, section 7.3; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 13, Organisms and Populations, section 13.1; Gujarat Biotechnology Research Centre, Mangroves, research-area overview, consulted 3 November 2026; Wildlife Institute of India, Ecology and Management of Banni Grasslands of Kachchh, Gujarat, introductory habitat description.]

pictures.caption: Dry grasslands and scrub habitats support organisms adapted to limited and seasonal water availability.

title: Habitats, Environmental Factors and Biological Adaptations

body:
From an individual organism to an ecosystem

Ecology is the study of relationships among organisms and between organisms and their physical environment. These relationships can be examined at different levels.

  • Organism: One individual living being, such as a frog.
  • Population: Individuals of the same species occupying a particular area at a particular time.
  • Community: Populations of different species living and interacting in an area.
  • Ecosystem: A community together with the non-living surroundings and the interactions occurring between them.
  • Biosphere: The parts of Earth where life exists, considered collectively.

A pond ecosystem contains aquatic plants, algae, fish, insects, bacteria and other organisms, along with water, dissolved substances, sunlight and temperature conditions. An ecosystem is therefore more than a list of species: it includes how living and non-living components affect one another.

Producers, consumers and decomposers

Producers form organic food from inorganic materials. In familiar terrestrial ecosystems, green plants are the main producers. In many aquatic ecosystems, algae and phytoplankton are major producers.

Consumers obtain food by eating producers or other consumers. Herbivores are typically primary consumers, while carnivores feeding on herbivores are secondary consumers.

Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, break down dead organisms and organic wastes. By releasing simpler substances and mineral nutrients, they contribute to the return of nutrients to soil and water.

Food chains and trophic levels

A food chain represents a feeding sequence through which organic matter and energy pass from one organism to another. Consider grass consumed by a grasshopper, the grasshopper eaten by a frog, and the frog eaten by a snake.

Trophic levelOrganism in exampleRole
1GrassProducer
2GrasshopperPrimary consumer
3FrogSecondary consumer
4SnakeTertiary consumer

In this example, the producer occupies the first trophic level. The herbivore occupies the second, and the carnivore that eats the herbivore occupies the third.

A food web consists of interconnected food chains. It represents natural feeding relationships more realistically because many organisms have several food sources. A bird may function as a primary consumer when eating seeds but as a secondary consumer when eating herbivorous insects. Therefore, trophic level describes a feeding role, not a permanent rank assigned to every species.

Why energy decreases along a food chain

Energy is used by organisms for respiration, movement, maintenance and other activities. Some energy is released as heat, and not all the material consumed becomes new living tissue. Consequently, only a limited part of the energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next.

The school-level 10% law expresses a useful approximation: about 10% of the energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next. This is a teaching model rather than an exact percentage in every natural food chain.

For example, if producers in a simplified model contain 10,000 units of available energy, the corresponding primary, secondary and tertiary consumers may receive approximately 1,000, 100 and 10 units respectively.

Energy flow is different from nutrient cycling

Energy flows largely in one direction through an ecosystem: it enters through sources such as sunlight, is captured by producers, passes through consumers and is eventually dissipated as heat. It is not continuously recycled through the same food chain.

Nutrients are recycled. Plants take up mineral nutrients from soil or water. Animals obtain nutrients through food. Decomposers act on dead matter and wastes, making nutrients available again. The cycling of matter helps sustain continued biological production.

Ecological pyramids

Ecological pyramids compare the number of organisms, their biomass or their available energy at successive trophic levels. The pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy decreases as it passes to higher levels.

Pyramids of numbers and biomass are not always upright. For instance, a single large tree may support many insects. In some aquatic ecosystems, a relatively small standing biomass of rapidly reproducing phytoplankton can support a larger standing biomass of consumers.

An inverted pyramid of biomass does not imply that energy flows from consumers back into producers. Biomass and energy measure different properties.

Prelims focus

  • A population consists of members of the same species; a community includes different species.
  • An ecosystem includes living organisms, abiotic components and their interactions.
  • Producers occupy the first trophic level.
  • The 10% law is an approximate model of energy transfer.
  • The pyramid of energy is always upright; pyramids of numbers or biomass may be inverted.
  • Trap: Nutrients cycle through ecosystems, whereas energy does not cycle in the same way.

[NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 13, Organisms and Populations, introductory discussion; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 14, Ecosystem, sections 14.1–14.4 and discussion of ecological pyramids; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 15, Our Environment, section on food chains and trophic levels.]

pictures.alt: Energy decreases from grass at 10,000 units to grasshopper at about 1,000, frog at about 100 and snake at about 10, with roughly 10% transferred each time.
pictures.caption: Energy generally decreases at successive trophic levels.

pictures.alt: Nutrients cycle from soil and water through producers and consumers; decomposers break down dead matter and wastes, returning nutrients for reuse.
pictures.caption: Decomposition returns nutrients to the environment for reuse by producers.

title: Ecosystems, Food Chains and the Movement of Energy
